NSG 403400 Level Harmattan Semester
Maternal and Child Health Nursing I topics
Overview

NSG 403: Medical-Surgical Nursing Practicum III

3 Units · Clinical: PH 135

Learning Outcomes

At the end of the clinical posting, the student should be able to:

  1. Prepare patients for special laboratory investigations and procedures.
  2. Set up trays and trolleys for the care and management of patients.
  3. Provide nursing care to both medical and surgical patients under supervision.
  4. Perform assigned nursing procedures competently.
  5. Maintain accurate fluid intake and output charts.
  6. Administer and manage infusions, parenteral medications, and other prescribed medications under supervision.
  7. Provide appropriate patient counselling where necessary.

These postings enable students to integrate theoretical knowledge into clinical practice while enhancing their patient care skills.

NSG 403: Maternal and Child Health Nursing I

2 Units · Lecture Hours: LH 30

Learning Outcomes

At the end of the course, the student should be able to:

  1. Discuss the anatomical and physiological changes associated with pregnancy and childbirth.
  2. Apply knowledge of preconception care in caring for women and their families.
  3. Describe normal pregnancy, labour, and puerperium.
  4. Describe abnormal pregnancy, labour, and puerperium.
  5. Discuss family planning methods, including factors influencing their acceptance and choice.
  6. Apply acquired knowledge and skills to conduct physical health assessments, plan, and implement care for families in collaboration with other healthcare providers.
  7. Discuss the roles of the nurse and midwife in both clinical and community settings, including immunisation services.
  8. Describe the immediate and ongoing care of the newborn, including assessment, thermal care, cord care, feeding, birth-dose immunisation and recognition of danger signs.
  9. Apply the nursing process, including documentation, in planning and evaluating care for mothers and newborns.
  10. Provide health education, counselling and discharge instructions to mothers and families, using family-centred and culturally sensitive approaches.
Outcomes 8 to 10 are proposed additions to cover newborn care, the nursing process and health education. They are not from the original course outline, so check them with your lecturer.

  • Ethical and legal aspects of HIV/AIDS.
  • Quality of care in midwifery practice.

The continuum of careLO 1LO 7

Care should run continuously from before pregnancy through childbirth, infancy and childhood, rather than in fragmented services. Reducing maternal and childhood deaths and illness requires a continuum of care that spans pregnancy, childbirth, infancy, childhood, adolescence and adulthood.

Before pregnancy (preconception)LO 2

  • LO 2Interventions before pregnancy can improve the health and well-being of adolescents and of adult women and men, and lead to better outcomes in later pregnancies and for the child.
  • LO 2WHO’s preconception report lists packages of interventions in thirteen domains, covering health problems, risky behaviours and risk factors that contribute to maternal and childhood illness and death.

Pregnancy (antenatal care)

  • LO 3WHO’s 2016 model recommends at least eight antenatal contacts: one in the first trimester, two in the second and five in the third.
  • LO 4More contacts give more chances to detect and manage potential problems. A minimum of eight can reduce perinatal deaths compared with four.
  • LO 6The content of each contact should include blood pressure measurement, among other checks, plus counselling on healthy diet, optimal nutrition and physical activity.
  • LO 6Providers should ask all pregnant women about alcohol and other substance use as early as possible and at every antenatal visit.
  • LO 3WHO defines a positive pregnancy experience as keeping a healthy pregnancy for mother and baby, including preventing or treating risks, illness and death, and having an effective transition to positive labour and birth.
  • LO 7Antenatal care can be delivered by a broad range of cadres, from lay health workers to nurses, midwives and doctors.
  • LO 7Women should carry their own case notes during pregnancy to improve continuity and quality of care.

Delivery (childbirth)LO 3LO 4

Detail on this part was limited in the source material. See Normal labour below for the stages of labour.
  • WHO’s 2018 intrapartum guideline is the third in a set of three, alongside the antenatal and postnatal guidelines. It aims at a positive childbirth experience.
  • LO 3For newborn care at birth, WHO recommends delaying cord clamping to one to three minutes after birth for all births, along with skin-to-skin contact in the first hour.

After birth (postnatal period)

  • LO 3After an uncomplicated vaginal birth in a facility, healthy mothers and newborns should stay in the facility for at least 24 hours. After a home birth, the first postnatal contact should be as early as possible within 24 hours.
  • LO 3LO 7At least three more contacts are recommended: day 3 (48 to 72 hours), days 7 to 14, and six weeks after birth. Home visits in the first week are also recommended.
  • LO 6In the first 24 hours, a mother’s checks should include vaginal bleeding, uterine contraction, fundal height, temperature and pulse. Blood pressure is taken soon after birth, with a second reading within six hours if the first is normal.
  • LO 4Warning signs to assess in the newborn include no spontaneous movement, fever, low body temperature, and jaundice in the first 24 hours.
  • LO 4Screening for postnatal maternal depression and anxiety is recommended, with referral and management where needed.
  • LO 5Postnatal care includes exclusive breastfeeding counselling and access to postnatal contraception.
  • LO 7Care of the newborn includes promoting immunisation as per WHO guidelines. Vaccination at birth is also recommended.
  • LO 4LO 7Preterm and low-birth-weight babies should be identified immediately after birth and given special care.
  • LO 7Partner involvement is encouraged, for example by attending checkups and supporting the mother and baby.

Why it mattersLO 4

  • More than 3 in 10 women and babies worldwide do not get postnatal care in the first days after birth, which is when most maternal and infant deaths occur.
  • WHO estimates 810 women die each day from complications of pregnancy and childbirth, mostly preventable or treatable.

Preconception careLO 2

Preconception care is health care given to women and couples before pregnancy to find and reduce risks, so that conception happens when the woman is as healthy as possible. It is the start of the continuum of care described above.

What the nurse assesses

  • LO 6Obstetric history (previous losses, caesarean section, stillbirth, pre-eclampsia), medical and family history, and current medicines.
  • Nutrition and weight, immunisation status, infections, lifestyle (alcohol, tobacco) and psychosocial factors such as violence or lack of support.

What the nurse offers

  • Folic acid 400 µg daily from the time a woman starts trying to conceive until 12 weeks of pregnancy, to prevent neural tube defects. A higher dose (5 mg daily) is offered to women at higher risk, for example after a previous baby with a neural tube defect.
  • Screening and treatment or referral for HIV, syphilis and other STIs, hepatitis B and anaemia, and control of conditions such as diabetes and hypertension before conception.
  • Haemoglobin genotype testing and counselling, so couples know their sickle cell risk before they conceive.
  • Updating immunisations such as tetanus. Avoid pregnancy for a month after rubella or other live vaccines.
  • Advice to stop alcohol and tobacco, review medicines with the prescriber, reach a healthy weight and eat a varied diet.
  • LO 5Birth spacing: wait at least 24 months after a live birth, and at least 6 months after a miscarriage or abortion, before the next pregnancy. Counsel on family planning for this period.
  • LO 7Give this care at family planning, postnatal and immunisation visits, in the community and in schools, not only when a woman asks for it.

Anatomical and physiological changes in pregnancyLO 1

  • The changes affect nearly every organ system. They are driven by hormones from the placenta and by the mechanical needs of a growing fetus.
  • Pregnancy changes the endocrine, cardiovascular, pulmonary, renal, haematologic and gastrointestinal systems. Hormones, gestational age and fetal size all drive these changes.
  • The aim is to maximise nutrition and oxygen to the developing fetus. Most of the changes are in place by the end of the first trimester and only increase in size afterwards.

Cardiovascular and blood

  • LO 1Blood volume rises by about 40 to 50%. Plasma expands more than red cells, so the blood is diluted. Haematocrit falls from about 40% to about 34%, the “physiological anaemia of pregnancy”.
  • LO 1LO 4This dilution may reduce bleeding when the placenta separates, but it raises the risk of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism.
  • LO 1Some normal changes can look pathological on cardiovascular examination if you don’t know they are expected.

Heart, blood pressure and clottingLO 1

  • Cardiac output rises by about 30 to 50%. The rise starts in the first trimester and peaks in the late second or early third trimester. Stroke volume increases and the heart rate is 10 to 20 beats per minute faster than before pregnancy.
  • Blood pressure usually dips in the second trimester, because progesterone relaxes the blood vessels, and returns towards its pre-pregnancy level near term. A reading of 140/90 mmHg or more is not a normal change and needs follow-up.
  • LO 6Supine hypotension: late in pregnancy, lying flat on the back lets the uterus press on the inferior vena cava, so less blood returns to the heart. The woman feels faint, pale and sweaty. Help her onto her left side, and use a left tilt for examinations and in labour.
  • LO 4Clotting factors, especially fibrinogen, rise and fibrinolysis falls, so pregnancy is a hypercoagulable state. This helps control bleeding at delivery but adds to the risk of deep vein thrombosis, together with slowed blood return from the legs.
  • The white cell count and the ESR rise, so a raised ESR is not a useful sign of infection in pregnancy.

Respiratory

  • Progesterone increases tidal volume. Respiratory alkalosis is compensated by the kidneys excreting bicarbonate, and the raised diaphragm changes lung volumes.
  • Oxygen demand rises, with a 40 to 50% increase in minute ventilation, mostly from a larger tidal volume rather than a faster rate.
  • The diaphragm rises about 4 cm and the chest widens, and oxygen use rises by about 20%. Many women feel breathless without any disease (physiological dyspnoea). Oestrogen engorges the nasal lining, so a blocked nose and nosebleeds are common.
  • LO 4The air left in the lungs after a normal breath out (functional residual capacity) falls by about 20%, so oxygen reserve is low and a pregnant woman becomes hypoxic quickly if she stops breathing or is under anaesthesia.

Renal

  • Renal blood flow and glomerular filtration rate rise by about 50%. Progesterone and relaxin dilate the urinary tract.
  • Mild physiological hydronephrosis can be seen as the uterus compresses the ureters at the pelvic brim.
  • Urinary frequency is common in early pregnancy, eases in the second trimester and returns late in pregnancy when the baby’s head engages and presses on the bladder.
  • Glucose is often found in the urine because filtration rises faster than the tubules can reabsorb it. Glycosuria alone does not diagnose diabetes.
  • LO 4LO 6Dilated ureters slow urine flow, which raises the risk of urinary tract infection and pyelonephritis. Test the urine at antenatal visits for protein, glucose and signs of infection.

Uterus, cervix, vagina and ovariesLO 1

  • The uterus grows from about 60 to 70 g to about 1 kg at term, and its capacity from a few millilitres to about 5 litres. Oestrogen and progesterone make the muscle fibres grow (hypertrophy) in early pregnancy, then stretching takes over.
  • It rises out of the pelvis at about 12 weeks. Fundal height is a useful landmark: just above the symphysis pubis at 12 weeks, midway to the umbilicus at 16 weeks, at the umbilicus at about 20 weeks and at the xiphisternum at 36 weeks. It falls a little at 38 to 40 weeks as the head engages (lightening). Between about 24 and 36 weeks the height in centimetres roughly equals the weeks of gestation, give or take 2 cm.
  • LO 4Uterine blood flow rises from about 50 mL a minute to about 500 to 700 mL a minute at term. That is why bleeding is brisk if the uterus fails to contract after the placenta separates.
  • Braxton Hicks contractions are painless, irregular tightenings that start early, are noticed in the second half of pregnancy and strengthen near term. Unlike true labour, they do not change the cervix.
  • The cervix softens from about 6 weeks (Goodell’s sign) and the lower part of the uterus softens (Hegar’s sign). The cervix and vagina turn bluish-violet from increased blood supply (Chadwick’s sign). A mucous plug seals the cervical canal and is lost later as the “show”.
  • The vagina thickens and produces more white, non-itchy discharge (leucorrhoea). The vaginal pH becomes more acidic, which protects against many infections but favours thrush (candida).
  • Ovulation stops. The corpus luteum makes progesterone until the placenta takes over at about 10 to 12 weeks.

BreastsLO 1

  • The breasts enlarge and tingle early in pregnancy. The nipples and areolae darken, the Montgomery’s tubercles stand out and the veins become visible.
  • Colostrum can be expressed from about 16 weeks. Milk is not secreted until after birth, because high oestrogen and progesterone block the effect of prolactin. Their fall after the placenta is delivered starts lactation.

HormonesLO 1

  • hCG is made by the early placenta. It peaks at about 8 to 10 weeks, keeps the corpus luteum making progesterone until the placenta takes over, and is the basis of pregnancy tests. It is linked with nausea and vomiting.
  • Progesterone relaxes smooth muscle in the uterus, gut, ureters and blood vessels. It also raises body temperature slightly and drives deeper breathing.
  • Oestrogen grows the uterus and breast ducts, increases blood flow and fluid retention, raises clotting factors and darkens the skin.
  • Human placental lactogen (hPL) makes the mother more resistant to insulin from mid-pregnancy, so more glucose reaches the baby. This explains why gestational diabetes shows up in the second half.
  • Relaxin softens ligaments and the cervix.
  • Prolactin rises through pregnancy and prepares the breasts. The thyroid may enlarge slightly, and total thyroxine rises because binding proteins rise while free hormone stays normal. Cortisol, aldosterone and renin rise, which helps the body retain salt and water.

Digestive systemLO 1

  • Nausea and vomiting (“morning sickness”) affect many women from about 4 to 16 weeks and usually settle by 20 weeks. Rising hCG is linked to it. Persistent severe vomiting is hyperemesis gravidarum (see the complications section).
  • Progesterone loosens the lower oesophageal sphincter and slows gut movement, and the uterus pushes the stomach upwards. The result is heartburn and constipation, and the extra water absorbed from the colon hardens the stool. Haemorrhoids are common.
  • The gallbladder empties slowly, which raises the risk of gallstones and of cholestasis (itching without a rash).
  • The gums become more vascular and bleed easily. Appetite rises, and cravings and food aversions are common.

Bones, joints, posture and skinLO 1

  • Relaxin and progesterone loosen the ligaments and joints. The pubic symphysis and sacroiliac joints widen a little, which helps the pelvis expand for birth but can cause pelvic girdle pain.
  • The growing uterus moves the centre of gravity forward. Women lean back (lordosis), which causes backache and a waddling gait, and the rectus abdominis muscles may separate (diastasis recti). Leg cramps are common.
  • Skin pigmentation increases: linea nigra, darker areolae and chloasma (the “mask of pregnancy”). Striae gravidarum appear on the abdomen, breasts and thighs from stretching. Oestrogen causes spider naevi and palmar erythema. Most of these fade after birth.

Weight and metabolismLO 1

  • The basal metabolic rate rises, and fat is stored early in pregnancy as an energy reserve for later pregnancy and lactation.
  • Weight gain is small in the first trimester (about 1 to 2 kg) and then about 0.4 kg a week for a woman of normal weight. For a normal pre-pregnancy BMI the usual target is about 11.5 to 16 kg in total. Many textbooks quote an average of 10 to 12.5 kg. Women who are underweight need to gain more, and women with obesity less.
  • LO 6Weigh at every antenatal visit. A weight plateau, a sudden large gain or new swelling of the face and hands needs assessment, because it can signal pre-eclampsia (see the abnormal pregnancy section). Mild ankle swelling by evening is common and normal.
  • After meals, blood glucose is higher than before pregnancy and fasting glucose is lower, because of insulin resistance and the baby’s steady glucose demand.

Changes during labour and childbirthLO 1LO 3

  • Contractions begin near the top of the uterus and are strongest and longest there (fundal dominance), while the lower segment stays relatively passive. Between contractions the upper muscle does not return to its full length (retraction), so the upper segment thickens and the lower segment thins and stretches.
  • The cervix shortens (effaces) and then dilates to 10 cm. In a first pregnancy, effacement is usually well advanced before dilatation. In later pregnancies the two happen together. The mucous plug is lost with a little blood (the show) and the membranes rupture.
  • Cardiac output, pulse and blood pressure rise further with contractions. Cardiac output is highest straight after birth, when blood from the emptied, contracted uterus returns to the circulation. This autotransfusion is well tolerated by a healthy woman but is a risk in heart disease.
  • LO 6Stomach emptying slows in labour, and pain and opioids slow it further. If general anaesthesia is needed, food in the stomach raises the risk of vomiting and aspiration.

Why nurses need thisLO 1LO 6

  • Knowing the normal changes helps recognise pathology and anticipate complications.

Normal labourLO 3

WHO’s 2018 intrapartum guideline covers essential care throughout labour and childbirth, plus interventions specific to the first, second and third stages.

What is normal labour?LO 3

Labour is the process by which the baby, placenta and membranes are expelled from the uterus through the birth canal. The WHO describes normal birth as spontaneous in onset, low risk at the start and throughout, with the baby born spontaneously head first (vertex) between 37 and 42 completed weeks, and mother and baby in good condition afterwards.

  • True labour: contractions are regular and become longer, stronger and closer together. They are felt in the back and abdomen, continue despite rest and walking, and bring progressive cervical effacement and dilatation, often with a show or rupture of membranes.
  • False labour (Braxton Hicks): contractions are irregular and short, felt low in the abdomen or groin, ease with rest, walking or fluids, and do not change the cervix.

The stages of labour at a glanceLO 3

StageBeginsEndsUsual durationMain care
First stage: latent phasePainful contractions with effacement and slow dilatationCervix at 5 cmNo standard duration. It varies widely between women.Welcome the woman and explain. Take history, maternal vital signs, abdominal examination and fetal heart. Encourage walking, fluids and support. Do not rush to intervene.
First stage: active phaseCervix at 5 cmFull dilatation (10 cm)Usually not beyond 12 hours in a first labour and 10 hours in later laboursStart the partograph or Labour Care Guide. Fetal heart every 15 to 30 minutes, contractions every 30 minutes, vaginal examination every 4 hours, maternal pulse, blood pressure and temperature at the intervals set by your unit. Keep the bladder empty, offer fluids and food, choice of position, pain relief and a companion.
Second stageFull dilatationBirth of the babyUsually within 3 hours in a first labour and 2 hours in later laboursSupport her own urge to push, with upright or lateral positions. Fetal heart every 5 minutes. Support the perineum. Dry the baby and place skin-to-skin, then delay cord clamping for 1 to 3 minutes.
Third stageBirth of the babyDelivery of placenta and membranesUsually within about 30 minutes with active management, and up to 60 minutes with physiological managementActive management: oxytocin 10 IU IM within a minute of birth, controlled cord traction, then check the placenta, uterine tone and perineum.
Fourth stageDelivery of placentaEnd of the first 1 to 2 hoursFirst 1 to 2 hours. Close monitoring continues through the first 24 hours.Check blood pressure, pulse, uterine tone and bleeding often (for example every 15 minutes in the first hour). Keep mother and baby together and start breastfeeding.

Older textbooks give different figures, for example an active phase starting at 3 or 4 cm, a 1 cm an hour rate of dilatation, and a set limit for the second stage. WHO’s 2018 guideline replaced these. Follow the definitions your lecturer and local protocol use in exams.

First stage in more detailLO 3LO 6

  • On admission, take the history, check the woman’s vital signs, examine the abdomen (lie, presentation and how much of the head is felt above the pelvis), listen to the fetal heart and test the urine. A vaginal examination checks the cervix, membranes, presentation, position and station. Start the partograph or Labour Care Guide in the active phase.
  • Near full dilatation (the transition), contractions are strongest. Many women feel nauseated, shaky and irritable and may want to push. Stay with her, reassure her and check that the cervix is fully dilated before she pushes.
  • Offer fluids and light food, help her to move and change position, encourage her to pass urine every 2 to 4 hours because a full bladder can slow descent, and keep her companion involved.

Second stage and the mechanism of labourLO 3

  • Signs of the second stage include an urge to push, a bulging perineum, a dilated anus and a visible head (crowning).
  • With the head presenting, the baby moves through the pelvis in a set order: engagement, descent, flexion, internal rotation, crowning and extension (the head is born), restitution, external rotation of the head as the shoulders rotate inside, and lateral flexion as the shoulders and body are born.
  • WHO recommends that women follow their own urge to push and choose their birth position. Warm compresses and hands-on support of the perineum can reduce perineal trauma. Routine episiotomy and pressure on the top of the uterus (fundal pressure) are not recommended.
  • The baby is dried and placed on the mother’s chest for skin-to-skin contact. See Topic 2 for newborn care at birth.

Third stageLO 3LO 4

  • Signs that the placenta has separated: the cord lengthens, there is a small gush of blood, and the uterus rises and becomes firm and rounded.
  • The placenta separates from the centre (Schultze method: shiny fetal surface delivered first, little visible bleeding until it is out) or from the edge (Matthews Duncan method: dull maternal surface delivered first, with bleeding earlier).
  • Active management of the third stage lowers the risk of postpartum haemorrhage. It is oxytocin 10 IU IM within a minute of birth after checking there is no second baby, and controlled cord traction with counter-traction on the uterus by a skilled attendant once the signs of separation appear. Then check that the uterus is firm and well contracted.
  • Examine the placenta and membranes to check they are complete, and count the cord vessels (two arteries and one vein). Missing tissue can cause bleeding. Examine the vagina and perineum for tears and estimate the blood loss.
  • If the placenta has not come out within about 30 minutes of active management, treat it as a retained placenta and refer, as described in the postpartum haemorrhage section.

Fourth stageLO 3LO 4

  • Postpartum haemorrhage is most likely in the first hour or two after the placenta is delivered, so observe closely. Check blood pressure, pulse, temperature, uterine tone (firm and central) and vaginal bleeding. Many units check every 15 minutes in the first hour and every 30 minutes in the second, so follow your local protocol.
  • Help her to pass urine, because a full bladder stops the uterus contracting well. Keep her clean, warm and comfortable, and help the baby to breastfeed within the first hour.
  • Record the birth, blood loss, placenta check, perineal findings and the baby’s condition, and complete the partograph. The mother and baby stay in the facility for at least 24 hours.

Recommended care across all stages

  • Continuous support for the woman
  • Monitoring maternal and fetal heart rate
  • Monitoring maternal blood pressure, pulse and temperature
  • Offering oral fluids and food
  • Pain relief, both non-drug and drug-based

Stage-specific care

  • First stage: the partograph is used in the latent and active phases, with vaginal examination to assess cervical dilatation.
  • Third stage: active management with oxytocin is recommended.

Respectful, supportive practices

  • Respectful maternity care
  • Labour and birth companionship
  • Effective communication
  • Choice of birth position
  • Choice of pain relief

Change to the partograph

The 2018 guideline changed the partograph. WHO made a “next-generation” partograph, the Labour Care Guide, which drops the 1 cm per hour alert and action lines.

Normal puerperium (postnatal period)LO 3

The puerperium runs from the delivery of the placenta until about 6 weeks (42 days) after birth, when the reproductive organs have returned approximately to their non-pregnant state. It is often divided into the immediate period (first 24 hours), the early period (up to 7 days) and the late period (to 6 weeks).

Involution of the uterus and the lochiaLO 3

Time after birthUterusLochia
Days 1 to 3 or 4Weighs about 1 kg. The fundus is at about the level of the umbilicus and falls roughly 1 cm (a finger breadth) a day.Lochia rubra: red and bloody, with small clots, decidua and membrane fragments.
About day 4 to 10About 500 g by the end of the first week. The fundus is midway between the umbilicus and the symphysis pubis by about day 5.Lochia serosa: pink to brown, thinner and watery.
About day 10 to 14No longer felt above the symphysis pubis. It is now a pelvic organ.Lochia alba: yellowish-white, with white cells, mucus and decidual cells. It can last up to about 6 weeks.
6 weeksAbout 50 to 100 g, close to non-pregnant size.Usually stopped.
  • The uterus shrinks because muscle fibres are broken down (autolysis) and blood supply is reduced as the uterus contracts and retracts. The inner lining regrows by about day 10, and the placental site heals fully by about 6 weeks.
  • Afterpains are cramping pains from uterine contractions. They are commoner in women who have had several babies and in breastfeeding women, because suckling releases oxytocin.
  • LO 4LO 6The fundus falling slower than expected, heavy or bright red bleeding returning, large clots, or an offensive smell can mean retained tissue or infection. A soft, high or tender uterus needs the same action.

Other body systemsLO 3

  • Cervix, vagina and perineum: the cervix is soft and open at first, and the internal os closes in about 2 weeks. The outer opening stays slit-like after a vaginal birth. The vagina is swollen and smooth at first, and its folds (rugae) return by about 3 weeks. Perineal tears and episiotomy usually heal within 2 to 3 weeks.
  • Urinary tract: there is a diuresis over the first days as extra fluid is lost. The bladder is often swollen and less sensitive after birth, so a woman may not feel the need to pass urine. Encourage her to pass urine within about 6 hours.
  • Bowels: constipation is common because of reduced food intake, fear of pain and perineal discomfort. Fluids, fibre and walking help.
  • Blood and circulation: blood volume returns towards normal over the first weeks. Clotting stays raised for about 6 weeks, so the risk of deep vein thrombosis persists. The white cell count is high in the first days.
  • Abdominal wall: the muscles are slack and may remain separated for some weeks. Striae fade to silvery lines.
  • Hormones and periods: oestrogen and progesterone fall sharply once the placenta is delivered. In women who do not breastfeed, periods usually return at about 6 to 8 weeks, but ovulation can occur before the first period, as early as about 4 weeks after birth.

LactationLO 3

  • After the placenta is delivered, the fall in progesterone and oestrogen lets prolactin start milk production. Colostrum is produced in the first days. The milk “comes in” (transitional milk) at about days 2 to 5, and mature milk follows by about 2 weeks.
  • Prolactin makes the milk, and oxytocin makes it flow (the let-down or milk ejection reflex). The baby’s suckling releases both. Early, frequent feeds and a good latch build the supply and prevent engorgement. See Topics 2 and 4 for feeding and drugs in breastfeeding.

Psychological adaptationLO 3LO 4

  • Rubin describes the mother’s adjustment in three phases: taking-in (first 2 to 3 days, when she is passive, tired and needs to talk about the birth), taking-hold (she becomes active and wants to learn baby care) and letting-go (she accepts her new role).
  • Postnatal blues are common around days 3 to 5, with tearfulness, mood swings and anxiety, and settle within about 2 weeks with rest and support. Low mood that lasts longer, or any thoughts of harming herself or the baby, needs referral. Screening for postnatal depression and anxiety is recommended.

Postnatal care: the BUBBLE-HE checkLO 3LO 6

Check the mother’s temperature, pulse and blood pressure, then use this mnemonic to cover the rest of the examination. Contacts are at 24 hours, day 3, days 7 to 14 and 6 weeks, as set out under the continuum of care.

  • Breasts: fullness, nipples, redness or pain, and how the baby feeds.
  • Uterus: height of the fundus, firmness and tenderness.
  • Bladder: whether she is passing urine freely.
  • Bowels: when they last opened, and constipation or haemorrhoids.
  • Lochia: amount, colour, clots and smell.
  • Episiotomy or perineum: swelling, bruising, discharge, wound edges and pain.
  • Homans’ sign, meaning the legs: calf pain, swelling, redness or warmth that could be a deep vein thrombosis. Homans’ sign itself is not reliable, so look for these other signs.
  • Emotions: mood, sleep, bonding and support at home.

Health education and danger signsLO 4LO 10

  • Teach perineal and personal hygiene, a varied diet and plenty of fluids, rest, pelvic floor and leg exercises, exclusive breastfeeding, family planning and the baby’s immunisation and follow-up dates. See Topic 2 for discharge teaching.
  • Tell her to return or call at once for heavy or increasing vaginal bleeding or large clots, fever or shivering, foul-smelling discharge, severe or increasing abdominal pain, severe headache with blurred vision, fits, calf pain or swelling, chest pain or difficulty breathing, a red, hot, painful breast, or feeling very low or hopeless.

Abnormal pregnancy, labour and puerperiumLO 4

The main life-threatening complications are haemorrhage, obstructed labour, eclampsia and puerperal sepsis. In Africa, haemorrhage and hypertension together account for almost 50% of maternal deaths.

Pre-eclampsia and eclampsia

  • Pre-eclampsia is diagnosed in a woman with hypertension, protein in the urine and/or severe oedema. It becomes eclampsia when convulsions occur.
  • LO 6Pre-eclampsia is often symptomless, so it can’t be diagnosed by interview alone. That makes routine blood pressure and urine checks essential.
  • Signs of severe pre-eclampsia include blood pressure of 160/110 mmHg or more, severe headache with visual disturbance, and epigastric pain.

Postpartum haemorrhage

  • It is often caused by uterine atony, the uterus failing to contract.
  • Other causes are genital tract trauma and retained placenta.

Obstructed and prolonged labour

  • It can happen if the baby’s head is too large or the position is abnormal. Unmanaged, it can lead to prolonged labour, uterine rupture, and fetal and maternal death.
  • Prolonged labour is defined as lasting longer than 24 hours.

Puerperal sepsis

  • It is a severe infection of the uterus after delivery. Warning signs include fever, shivering and abdominal pain.

ResponseLO 4LO 7

  • Midwives and community-level staff give pre-referral management of severe complications, such as obstructed labour and severe bleeding. Specialised facilities treat them with caesarean section, transfusion and similar care.

More complications of pregnancy and labourLO 4

The complications above cause most deaths, but nurses also meet the conditions below. In each case the nurse recognises the problem early, gives first-line care, refers without delay and keeps clear records.

Bleeding in early pregnancy

  • Abortion (miscarriage) is loss of the pregnancy before the baby can survive. Types are threatened, inevitable, incomplete, complete, missed and septic. Suspect it with bleeding, cramping lower abdominal pain and an open cervix. Check vital signs, estimate blood loss and refer for evacuation if incomplete.
  • Ectopic pregnancy is implantation outside the uterus, most often in the fallopian tube. Risk factors include previous pelvic infection, tubal surgery and previous ectopic pregnancy. Suspect it with missed period, lower abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding. Rupture causes shock, so start IV access and refer as an emergency.

Antepartum haemorrhage (bleeding after the 28th week, before delivery)

  • Placenta praevia: painless, bright red, often recurrent bleeding, with a soft, non-tender uterus.
  • Abruptio placentae: painful bleeding, which may be concealed, with a hard, tender uterus and shock out of proportion to visible loss. Hypertension and trauma are risk factors.
  • LO 6Do not perform a vaginal examination if there is bleeding in late pregnancy, because it can provoke severe haemorrhage in placenta praevia. Check vital signs and fetal heart, set up an IV line and refer.

Anaemia in pregnancy

  • Anaemia is a haemoglobin below 11 g/dL (110 g/L). Common causes are iron deficiency, malaria, hookworm and sickle cell disease.
  • Prevent it with 30 to 60 mg of elemental iron and 400 µg of folic acid daily. If anaemia is found, iron is raised to 120 mg daily until haemoglobin is normal, then the standard dose continues.
  • Severe anaemia raises the risk of heart failure, preterm birth and death from bleeding at delivery.

Malaria in pregnancy

  • Prevention has three parts: sleeping under an insecticide-treated net, intermittent preventive treatment with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (IPTp-SP), and prompt treatment of illness.
  • IPTp-SP is given from 13 weeks at each antenatal contact, at least one month apart, ideally as directly observed therapy. One dose is three tablets of 500 mg/25 mg.
  • Folic acid at 5 mg or more daily should not be given with SP, because it weakens SP’s effect.

Other conditions

  • Hyperemesis gravidarum: severe persistent vomiting with dehydration, ketones in the urine and weight loss. Rehydrate, give small frequent meals and refer if the woman cannot keep fluids down.
  • Gestational diabetes: glucose intolerance first found in pregnancy. It raises the risk of a large baby, shoulder dystocia and newborn hypoglycaemia. Screen, advise on diet and monitor.
  • Preterm labour is labour before 37 completed weeks. Premature rupture of membranes is rupture before labour starts, and it raises the risk of infection. Avoid repeated vaginal examinations, use sterile pads, monitor temperature and fetal heart, and refer.
  • Malpresentation (breech, transverse lie, brow or face) is suspected when the head is not engaged or the lie is abnormal. Refer to a facility able to do a caesarean section. If the cord prolapses, place the woman in the knee-chest position, keep the presenting part off the cord and arrange emergency transfer.
  • LO 7Midwives and community staff give pre-referral care, then arrange transport and record what was done.

Family planning methods and what influences choiceLO 5

  • Postpartum women have among the greatest unmet need for family planning. Postpartum family planning means avoiding closely spaced and unplanned pregnancies by using family planning services in the first year after delivery.
  • The antenatal and postnatal contacts are the best time to counsel. Postpartum is a time of frequent contact with the health system, which gives a chance to promote birth spacing.
  • Methods in use include pills, injectables, copper intrauterine devices, implants and emergency contraception. In a Jos, Nigeria study, the most preferred postpartum methods were the subdermal implant, then injectables, then the intrauterine device.

Contraceptive methods at a glanceLO 5

Effectiveness is WHO’s figure: pregnancies per 100 women in the first year, as commonly used / with consistent and correct use. Lower is better. WHO’s medical eligibility criteria give the final word on who can use each method, so check them and your national guideline before advising.

Combined injectables, the patch and the vaginal ring also exist but are less used in Nigeria. They are oestrogen-containing methods, so the same cautions after childbirth apply.

Choosing a method after childbirthLO 5LO 3

  • Counsel during antenatal care, so that a woman can choose before she is tired or in pain. Use the GATHER steps: Greet, Ask, Tell, Help, Explain and Return.
  • The choice must be informed and voluntary. Involving the partner is encouraged, because spousal refusal is a common reason for not using a method (see below), but check your national policy on what is required.
  • A breastfeeding mother can use LAM for up to 6 months, and can use progestogen-only methods or an IUD, which do not reduce milk. Avoid the combined pill. Add condoms if she or her partner may be at risk of STIs.
  • Fertility can return before the first period. A woman who is not fully breastfeeding can become pregnant as early as about 4 weeks after birth, so she should start a method by then.
  • WHO’s medical eligibility criteria sort each condition into four categories for each method. Category 1: no restriction. Category 2: benefits usually outweigh risks. Category 3: risks usually outweigh benefits. Category 4: unacceptable health risk, so do not use.

Factors that reduce acceptance

  • Partner and family approval, and past experience with methods, influence the decision to adopt.
  • In Jos, reasons for not using a method were spousal refusal, effect on fertility, desire for more children and religious beliefs.
  • Elsewhere, fear of side effects, lack of knowledge and husband opposition mattered, and wanting a pregnancy or preferring a male child was the leading reason.
  • A common misconception is that no contraception is needed after childbirth.

Factors that increase acceptance

  • Exposure to counselling, past contraceptive use and resumption of sex were linked to higher acceptance, while age under 25 and first-time mothers had lower odds.
  • Counselling during antenatal and postnatal care helps women make informed choices.
Notes on the sources. Most of this is WHO guidance, plus a few journal studies. The physiology notes also draw on lecture slides and student assignments, so check them against your course textbook before using them in exams or write-ups. Nigerian nursing programmes often use their own protocols (for example on the partograph), so your lecturer’s notes or Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria materials may differ in detail.
Notes on the drafted additions. The contraceptive table uses WHO’s effectiveness figures and its IUD and family planning fact sheets, with postpartum timing taken from WHO’s medical eligibility criteria. The stages of labour follow WHO’s 2018 intrapartum guideline for definitions and durations. The puerperium and the pregnancy physiology sections are standard midwifery textbook content that did not come from your original sources. Check the figures (for example uterine weight, weight gain, lochia timings and the BUBBLE-HE mnemonic) against your lecturer’s notes and the Nigerian national family planning guideline before using them in exams.

Nursing care of mothers, newborns, and families.

NSG 403: Maternal and Child Health Nursing I · Topic 2 of 13

Download practice pack:
On this pageImmediate care of the newborn at birthOngoing care of the newbornNewborn danger signsBirth-dose immunisation in NigeriaThe nursing process for mother and newbornHealth education, counselling and dischargeFamily-centred and culturally sensitive care

LO n tags show which course learning outcome each point supports (see the Overview tab). LO 8 to 10 are proposed additions.

Immediate care of the newborn at birthLO 8

WHO lists essential newborn care as immediate care at birth, thermal care, nurturing care, assessment of health problems, and recognition of and response to danger signs. It is needed in the facility and at home.

  • Delay cord clamping to one to three minutes for all births, as in Topic 1, while starting essential newborn care.
  • Dry the baby thoroughly, assess breathing, and place the baby skin-to-skin with the mother in the first hour.
  • Help the mother start breastfeeding within one hour of birth.
  • Apgar score: appearance (colour), pulse, grimace (reflex response), activity (tone) and respiration, each scored 0 to 2, at 1 and 5 minutes. A total of 7 to 10 is reassuring. Never delay resuscitation to wait for a score.

Ongoing care of the newbornLO 8

Thermal care and bathing

  • Keep the baby dry, wrapped and covered, ideally skin-to-skin. A normal axillary temperature is 36.5 to 37.5 °C.
  • Delay the first bath for at least 6 hours, and to 24 hours where possible. Dry and dress the baby straight after any bath.

Cord care

  • Clean, dry cord care is recommended. Keep the stump loosely covered, fold the nappy below it, and wash hands before and after handling it.
  • Daily 4% chlorhexidine in the first week is advised only where harmful substances (for example animal dung) are commonly put on the cord.
  • Signs of infection to report: redness spreading from the stump, swelling, pus, a foul smell or fever.

Feeding and observation

  • LO 8LO 10Breastfeed within the first hour and exclusively for the first 6 months. Give nothing else, not even water, milk or herbal teas.
  • Expect about 8 to 12 feeds in 24 hours. Observe temperature, breathing, feeding, colour, urine and meconium, and weigh the baby.
  • Give vitamin K and eye prophylaxis according to your facility’s protocol.

Newborn danger signsLO 8LO 7

Assess for danger signs at every postnatal contact, and teach families to seek care early if they see any.

  • Not feeding well, convulsions, or movement only when stimulated.
  • Fast breathing (60 or more breaths per minute) or severe chest indrawing.
  • Fever (37.5 °C or above) or low temperature (below 35.5 °C).
  • Jaundice in the first 24 hours, as in Topic 1.
  • A red, swollen or pus-draining cord stump.

Birth-dose immunisation in NigeriaLO 7LO 8

  • The routine schedule gives BCG, OPV0 and hepatitis B (HepB 0) at birth. The next doses are at 6 weeks: OPV1, Pentavalent 1 and PCV1.
  • The hepatitis B birth dose should be given within 24 hours of delivery (0.5 mL intramuscular, anterolateral right thigh).
  • BCG (0.05 mL intradermal, left upper arm) is preferably given within two weeks of birth but can be given later in infancy.
  • Record every dose on the child’s immunisation card and tell the mother when to return. Timely birth doses are often missed, so check before discharge.

The nursing process for mother and newbornLO 9LO 6

Use the five steps: assessment, nursing diagnosis, planning (goals), implementation and evaluation. Write goals that are measurable and have a time frame. Record each finding and action with date, time and signature, and revise the plan when evaluation shows the goal is not met.

StepMother, postnatal day 1Newborn, day 1
AssessmentVital signs, fundal height and tone, lochia, perineum, bladder, breasts and feeding, mood, support at home.Temperature, breathing, heart rate, colour, tone, weight, feeding, cord, urine and meconium.
Nursing diagnosisRisk for postpartum haemorrhage related to uterine atony; acute perineal pain related to tissue trauma.Risk for impaired thermoregulation related to immature heat control and wet skin; risk for cord infection related to the open stump.
GoalFundus stays firm and lochia within expected amount through the first 24 hours. Pain rated tolerable within 1 hour of analgesia.Axillary temperature stays 36.5 to 37.5 °C. Baby feeds at least 8 times in 24 hours. Cord stays clean and dry.
ImplementationCheck fundus and lochia at set times and massage if boggy; help her empty her bladder; give prescribed analgesia; teach perineal hygiene and what to report.Skin-to-skin, cap and wrap, delay the bath, help with latch, keep the cord clean and dry, wash hands, give birth-dose vaccines.
EvaluationFundus firm, lochia moderate, pain tolerable. Escalate if a pad is soaked in an hour.Temperature in range, feeding well, cord dry. Escalate at once if any danger sign appears.

Health education, counselling and dischargeLO 10LO 7

  • Assess what the woman and her family already know and what they want to learn. Use plain language, preferably her own, and involve her partner or the person who will help at home.
  • Use teach-back: ask her to explain or demonstrate in her own words, for example how to position the baby at the breast, then correct and repeat.
  • Mother’s danger signs: heavy bleeding (a pad soaked in an hour), fever, severe headache or blurred vision, severe abdominal pain, foul-smelling discharge, calf pain or swelling, convulsions and difficulty breathing.
  • Newborn: danger signs, exclusive breastfeeding, cord care, warmth, hygiene, the immunisation card and when to return.
  • LO 5LO 3Postnatal visit schedule from Topic 1, and birth spacing with postpartum family planning options.
  • Rest, nutrition, perineal and breast care, and where to go in an emergency.

Family-centred and culturally sensitive careLO 10

  • Treat the family as the unit of care. Assess its strengths, its support, and who influences decisions, such as the partner or an elder.
  • Support bonding, keep mother and baby together, and protect privacy and dignity, as in respectful maternity care.
  • Ask about local beliefs and practices without judgement. Sort them into helpful, harmless or harmful, encourage the first two, and negotiate a safe alternative to a harmful one with the woman and family.
  • LO 9Work with the team, including community health workers, doctors and social support, and refer early when danger signs appear.
Notes on the sources. Newborn care, cord care and postnatal content follow WHO guidance. Immunisation details follow Nigeria’s routine schedule. Apgar scoring, normal ranges, vitamin K and the care plan examples come from standard nursing teaching, so check them against your course textbook, your lecturer’s notes and Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria protocols before using them in exams.

Drugs used in midwifery practice.

NSG 403: Maternal and Child Health Nursing I · Topic 3 of 13

Download practice pack:
On this pageSafe drug use in midwifery practiceKey drugs at a glanceDrugs for preventing and treating postpartum haemorrhageMagnesium sulfate: monitoring and toxicityOther drugs you will meetCalculating dosesTeaching the woman about her medicines

LO n tags show which course learning outcome each point supports (see the Overview tab). No course outcome covers drugs directly, so these tags show where drug use supports the existing outcomes.

Safe drug use in midwifery practiceLO 6LO 9LO 10

Many drugs cross the placenta or enter breast milk, so give a drug only when it is needed, in the smallest effective dose, and only within your scope of practice, on a prescription or an approved protocol.

  • Check the right woman, drug, dose, route, time and documentation, plus the reason for the drug and the woman’s response. Read the label and expiry date, and check allergies and whether she is pregnant or breastfeeding.
  • Calculate doses carefully, have a second person check high-risk drugs such as magnesium sulfate and oxytocin infusions, and record the drug, dose, route, time and your signature straight after giving it.
  • Watch for effects and side effects, report them, and know the antidote or emergency response before you start.
  • Doses in these notes come from WHO and other guidelines used for study. In practice, follow your facility protocol, the prescriber’s order and your council’s scope of practice.

Key drugs at a glanceLO 3LO 4LO 8

DrugUsed forUsual dose in the sourcesKey nursing checks
OxytocinPrevent postpartum haemorrhage (PPH); treat uterine atonyPrevention: 10 IU IM or IV once the baby is born. Treatment: IV infusion, 10 to 40 IU in 500 to 1000 mLExclude a second baby first. Never give before the baby is born. Check blood pressure and uterine tone
ErgometrinePPH when oxytocin is unavailable or has failed0.2 mg IMDo not give in hypertension, pre-eclampsia, eclampsia or heart disease
MisoprostolPrevent PPH where oxytocin is unavailable; treat PPHPrevention: 400 or 600 µg orally. Treatment: 800 µg sublinguallyShivering and fever are common. Community health workers may give it where no skilled attendant is present
Tranexamic acidTreat PPH1 g IV over 10 minutes, within 3 hours of birth. Repeat once if bleeding continues after 30 minutes or restarts within 24 hoursGive slowly, record the time of birth and of the dose
Magnesium sulfatePrevent and treat seizures in severe pre-eclampsia and eclampsia4 g IV over 15 to 20 minutes, then 10 g IM (5 g in each buttock), then 5 g IM every 4 hours. Or IV loading then 1 to 2 g per hourCheck reflexes, breathing and urine output before each dose. Keep calcium gluconate ready
Calcium gluconateAntidote for magnesium toxicity1 g (10 mL of 10%) IV, slowly over about 3 minutesGive slowly to avoid hypotension and a slow heart rate
DexamethasoneMature the baby’s lungs when preterm birth is imminent6 mg IM every 12 hours for 4 doses, at 24 to 34 weeksGive on the prescriber’s order and complete the course if birth is delayed
Vitamin KPrevent newborn bleedingUsually 1 mg IM at birth, per local protocolRecord it on the baby’s chart
Anti-D immunoglobulinPrevent Rhesus sensitisationGiven IM after birth of an Rh-positive baby to an Rh-negative mother, within 72 hoursConfirm both blood groups before giving

Drugs for preventing and treating postpartum haemorrhageLO 3LO 4

  • Oxytocin is the first choice for preventing PPH after every birth, and IV oxytocin is the first-line treatment when it occurs. Keep oxytocin in the refrigerator unless the label says otherwise, and do not give a fast IV bolus because it can drop the blood pressure.
  • Ergometrine is a second choice. It narrows blood vessels, so it is unsafe when blood pressure is high.
  • Misoprostol is used where oxytocin or skilled attendants are not available. It does not need refrigeration.
  • Tranexamic acid is not a uterotonic. It reduces bleeding and is added to the treatment package within 3 hours of birth.
  • LO 6Alongside the drugs, rub up the uterus, empty the bladder, estimate blood loss, check pulse and blood pressure, set up an IV line, and call for help or refer. PPH is blood loss of more than 500 mL in 24 hours after vaginal birth.

Magnesium sulfate: monitoring and toxicityLO 4LO 6

Magnesium sulfate is the drug of choice to stop and prevent seizures in eclampsia. It is more effective than phenytoin.

  • Before each dose check that the knee jerk (patellar reflex) is present, breathing is at least 16 per minute, and urine output is at least 30 mL per hour. If any check fails, hold the dose and call for help.
  • Early signs of toxicity are loss of the knee jerk, drowsiness, slurred speech and a slow heart rate. Breathing below 12 per minute is respiratory depression.
  • If toxicity is suspected, stop magnesium sulfate, give oxygen and give 1 g calcium gluconate slowly IV. Seizures may recur after the antidote.
  • Baby effects: floppiness and breathing problems can occur if the mother was treated close to birth.
  • It is usually continued for 24 hours after birth or the last seizure, per protocol. Record each check.
  • Blood pressure drugs such as labetalol, nifedipine or hydralazine are chosen by the prescriber for severe hypertension (160/110 mmHg or more). The nurse monitors blood pressure closely and watches for a sudden fall.

Other drugs you will meetLO 4LO 8LO 5

  • Antenatal corticosteroids: dexamethasone 6 mg IM every 12 hours for 4 doses, or betamethasone 12 mg IM every 24 hours for 2 doses, for women at risk of preterm birth between 24 and 34 weeks.
  • Iron with folic acid, folic acid before conception, and IPTp-SP for malaria are covered in the preconception and complications sections of Topic 1. Do not combine folic acid 5 mg or more with SP.
  • Antibiotics for premature rupture of membranes, puerperal sepsis or cord infection are given on the prescriber’s order after taking cultures or samples where possible.
  • Tetanus toxoid vaccine is given in pregnancy per the immunisation schedule. Avoid live vaccines during pregnancy.
  • Pain relief in labour and after birth, including paracetamol and pethidine, is covered in Topic 4. Opioids given close to birth can depress the baby’s breathing.

Calculating dosesLO 6

Dose to give = (dose ordered ÷ dose in the ampoule) × volume of the ampoule.

  • Dexamethasone 6 mg ordered; ampoule 4 mg in 1 mL: (6 ÷ 4) × 1 = 1.5 mL.
  • Magnesium sulfate 5 g ordered; ampoule 5 g in 10 mL (50%, 0.5 g per mL): 5 ÷ 5 × 10 = 10 mL. A deep IM injection of this size is usually given with a little local anaesthetic per protocol.
  • Always check your answer against a second person and the label before giving the drug.

Teaching the woman about her medicinesLO 10LO 6

  • Explain the name, purpose, how and when to take each drug, what side effects are common and which ones to report.
  • Advise on taking iron with food or a vitamin C drink, keeping all medicines out of children’s reach, and finishing a course of antibiotics.
  • Advise against self-medication and herbal preparations without advice from a health worker, especially in pregnancy and while breastfeeding.
  • Use teach-back, as in Topic 2, and write instructions down in a form she can use.
Notes on the sources. Doses for PPH, magnesium sulfate and antenatal corticosteroids follow WHO and other published guidelines. Vitamin K, anti-D, the dose calculations and the nursing checks come from standard nursing teaching. Doses vary between facilities, so check them against your lecturer’s notes, the national formulary and Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria protocols before using them in an exam or in practice.

Pain management in midwifery.

NSG 403: Maternal and Child Health Nursing I · Topic 4 of 13

Download practice pack:
On this pageUnderstanding labour painAssessing painNon-drug methods of pain reliefDrug methods of pain reliefChoosing and giving pain relief safelyEffects on the baby and breastfeedingPain after birthPreparing women for labour pain

LO n tags show which course learning outcome each point supports (see the Overview tab). No course outcome covers pain management directly, so these tags show where it supports the existing outcomes.

Understanding labour painLO 1LO 3LO 4

  • First-stage pain is visceral. It comes from cervical dilatation and uterine contractions, and is felt in the lower abdomen and back.
  • Second-stage pain is somatic. It comes from stretching of the vagina and perineum, and is sharper and more localised.
  • Pain varies widely between women. Fear, tension, tiredness, past experience, culture, a long labour and a lack of support all increase it. Fear raises tension, tension raises pain, and pain raises fear, so support and relaxation break the cycle.
  • LO 4Report pain that is out of keeping with the labour, for example constant severe pain with a hard, tender uterus (abruption) or pain with tenderness over a uterine scar.

Assessing painLO 6LO 9

  • Ask the woman to describe her pain: where it is, how strong (a 0 to 10 scale or a faces scale), how it comes and goes, and what helps. Do not judge by how loudly she cries.
  • Ask what she wants and what she planned. Pain relief depends on her preference.
  • Reassess after every intervention and record the score, the method, the drug and dose, the time and her response on the labour record or partograph.

Non-drug methods of pain reliefLO 3LO 10

WHO recommends offering the methods below to healthy women who request pain relief in labour, depending on their preference. They are safe for the baby and can be combined with drugs.

  • Continuous support and a companion of choice, with calm, respectful communication.
  • Relaxation: slow breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, music and mindfulness.
  • Manual techniques: massage, counter-pressure on the lower back and warm packs.
  • Upright positions, walking and movement, a birthing ball, a quiet room, enough fluids and a regularly emptied bladder.

Drug methods of pain reliefLO 3LO 6

MethodUseDetails in the sourcesKey nursing checks
ParacetamolMild to moderate pain, including perineal pain after birth500 mg to 1 g orally; do not exceed the daily limit on the labelAsk the time of the last dose and the total taken in 24 hours
IbuprofenPain after birth, with paracetamol, including when breastfeedingOral, as orderedAvoid in asthma triggered by NSAIDs, kidney problems, stomach ulcers or bleeding
PethidineModerate to severe labour pain50 to 100 mg IM, usually with an antiemetic. Repeat only per protocol after reviewCan cause drowsiness, nausea and breathing depression in mother and baby. Keep naloxone and resuscitation equipment ready
Entonox (50% nitrous oxide, 50% oxygen)Short-term relief in the active phaseSelf-administered by mask, started at the beginning of a contractionDizziness and nausea are common. The woman holds the mask herself
Lidocaine 1% infiltrationEpisiotomy and perineal repairGiven under the skin; stay within the limit in your protocolCheck allergy, aspirate before injecting, and watch for numb lips, a metallic taste, ringing ears or seizures
Pudendal blockSecond-stage perineal pain, instrumental birthGiven by a trained doctor or midwifeObserve for bleeding and discomfort afterwards
EpiduralStrong pain relief when a healthy woman requests itGiven by an anaesthetistCheck blood pressure and fetal heart before and after, give IV fluids, monitor the bladder and leg movement

Choosing and giving pain relief safelyLO 6LO 9LO 10

  • Respect the woman’s choice. Explain the benefits and risks of each option, get her consent and record it.
  • Consider the stage of labour, her health (for example, pre-eclampsia), the baby’s wellbeing, how close birth is, and what your facility can provide.
  • WHO does not recommend giving pain relief to prevent labour delay or reduce the need for augmentation. Never use it to speed up labour.
  • Check blood pressure, pulse, breathing and the fetal heart before and after a drug. Stay with the woman, keep her in a safe position with the bed rails up after sedation, and reassess after the drug has had time to work.
  • Some protocols avoid pethidine in severe pre-eclampsia, so the prescriber may choose another drug.

Effects on the baby and breastfeedingLO 8LO 10

  • Opioids cross the placenta. The effect on the baby depends on the dose and on how long before birth it was given, so pethidine is best avoided when birth is expected within a few hours.
  • After birth, watch the baby’s breathing, tone and suckling. A drowsy baby with slow or weak breathing needs breathing support first, and urgent help.
  • Naloxone reverses opioid depression in the baby and is given on the prescriber’s order. Doses differ between sources, so follow your local protocol.
  • Help the mother start breastfeeding early, with extra patience if the baby is sleepy.

Pain after birthLO 3LO 4LO 6LO 10

  • Common causes: afterpains from the uterus (stronger in women who have had several babies and when breastfeeding), perineal pain, haemorrhoids, breast engorgement, sore nipples and caesarean wound pain.
  • Use a stepwise approach. Start with paracetamol and add ibuprofen if needed. These are the first-line drugs when breastfeeding. Use stronger drugs only on the prescriber’s order.
  • Non-drug care: cold packs on the perineum in the first day, perineal hygiene, warm baths, a comfortable position for feeding, and a support pillow for the wound.
  • LO 4Report severe or rising perineal pain with swelling, fever or foul discharge, severe headache with visual disturbance, and calf pain or swelling.

Preparing women for labour painLO 10

  • Teach in antenatal classes: what labour pain is, breathing and relaxation, positions, and how a companion can help.
  • Discuss the options, and what each can and cannot do, before labour, and help her record her preferences in her birth plan.
  • Tell her pain relief is her choice and that she can change her mind.
Notes on the sources. Non-drug and drug options for labour follow the WHO 2018 intrapartum care recommendations. Pethidine, lidocaine and postpartum analgesia details come from national midwifery formularies and clinical guidance, and the nursing checks come from standard teaching. Newborn naloxone doses and lidocaine limits differ between sources, so follow your lecturer’s notes, the national formulary and local protocols.

Anatomy and physiology of the male and female reproductive systems.

NSG 403: Maternal and Child Health Nursing I · Topic 5 of 13

Download practice pack:
On this pageFemale external genitalia and the perineumFemale internal reproductive organsThe bony pelvis and pelvic floorThe breastsThe menstrual cycle and its hormonesFertilisation and implantationMale reproductive system

LO n tags show which course learning outcome each point supports (see the Overview tab). No course outcome covers non-pregnant anatomy directly, so LO 1 is used where the content is the baseline for the changes of pregnancy.

Female external genitalia and the perineumLO 1LO 6

  • The vulva includes the mons pubis, labia majora, labia minora, clitoris, and the vestibule. The vestibule contains the urethral opening, the vaginal opening (partly covered by the hymen) and the ducts of Bartholin’s glands.
  • The perineum is the area between the vaginal opening and the anus. Its central point, the perineal body, is where the bulbocavernosus and superficial transverse perineal muscles meet, and the levator ani muscles form the pelvic floor above it.
  • LO 3The perineal body stretches in the second stage and is the site of tears and episiotomy. The pudendal nerve (S2 to S4) supplies the perineum, which is why a pudendal block works in the second stage.
  • LO 6When examining the vulva, look at the skin, swelling, discharge, scars and any female genital mutilation, and keep the woman informed and covered.

Female internal reproductive organsLO 1LO 3

StructureKey factsWhy it matters
VaginaA muscular tube 7 to 9 cm long with folds (rugae). Its acidic pH (about 3.8 to 4.5) comes from lactic acid made by lactobacilliStretches in birth. The acidic pH protects against infection
UterusPear-shaped, about 7.5 cm long, 5 cm wide and 2.5 cm thick, weighing 50 to 60 g. Parts: fundus, body, isthmus and cervixHolds the pregnancy and contracts in labour. Fundal height is measured in pregnancy
Uterine wallPerimetrium (outer), myometrium (muscle) and endometrium (lining)The myometrium contracts in labour and after birth to control bleeding. The endometrium receives the embryo and sheds in menstruation
Uterine supportsBroad, round, uterosacral and cardinal ligaments, with the pelvic floor. The cardinal ligaments give the main supportWeakness can lead to prolapse
CervixLower neck of the uterus with an internal and an external os. Mucus changes with the cycleDilates in labour. Cervical mucus thickens with progesterone and hormonal contraception
Fallopian tubesAbout 10 cm long. Parts: interstitial, isthmus, ampulla and infundibulum with fimbriaeFertilisation occurs in the ampulla. Most ectopic pregnancies are tubal
OvariesAlmond-sized, hold follicles. Make oestrogen and progesterone and release an ovum each cycleHormones control the cycle. Ovulation is the basis of fertility awareness and hormonal contraception

The bony pelvis and pelvic floorLO 3LO 6

  • The true pelvis is the bony birth canal, with an inlet, a mid-cavity and an outlet. The false pelvis lies above it.
  • The most common female pelvis, the gynaecoid, is rounded and roomy and is best for vaginal birth.
  • LO 6Assess the pelvis and the fit of the baby’s head, and refer a woman if the pelvis may be too small for the baby.

The breastsLO 1LO 8

  • Each breast contains glandular tissue arranged in lobes of alveoli, milk ducts that widen into sinuses behind the nipple, and fat. The areola has Montgomery’s glands that keep the nipple supple.
  • Prolactin makes the alveoli produce milk, and oxytocin makes the surrounding cells contract so that milk is released (let-down).
  • LO 8Early and frequent suckling raises both hormones, and a good latch lets the baby remove milk.

The menstrual cycle and its hormonesLO 2LO 5

  • The hypothalamus releases GnRH, which makes the anterior pituitary release FSH and LH. FSH grows ovarian follicles, which make oestrogen. A surge of LH triggers ovulation. The corpus luteum then makes progesterone.
  • In a 28-day cycle: days 1 to 5 are menstruation, days 1 to 14 are the proliferative (follicular) phase as the endometrium thickens, ovulation is at about day 14, and days 15 to 28 are the secretory (luteal) phase.
  • If no pregnancy occurs the corpus luteum degenerates, hormone levels fall, and the endometrium sheds as menstruation.
  • The ovum survives about 24 hours and sperm up to about 5 days. Ovulation is about 14 days before the next period.
  • LO 5Combined pills, implants and injectables mainly stop ovulation and thicken cervical mucus. Fertility awareness methods depend on knowing the fertile days.

Fertilisation and implantationLO 1LO 2

  • Fertilisation occurs in the ampulla of the tube. The zygote divides as it travels to the uterus, becoming a morula and then a blastocyst.
  • The blastocyst implants in the endometrium about 6 to 7 days after fertilisation, usually in the upper uterus.
  • The trophoblast makes hCG, which maintains the corpus luteum and is the hormone found in pregnancy tests.
  • LO 4Implantation outside the uterus is an ectopic pregnancy, most often in the tube.

Male reproductive systemLO 2LO 5

StructureKey factsWhy it matters
TestesLie in the scrotum, 2 to 3 °C below body temperature, which sperm production needs. Seminiferous tubules make sperm, and Leydig cells make testosteroneHeat, such as undescended testes, lowers fertility
EpididymisCoiled tube on each testis where sperm mature and are storedSperm gain the ability to move here
Vas deferensCarries sperm from the epididymis towards the urethraVasectomy cuts or blocks it
Seminal vesicles, prostate, bulbourethral glandsAdd fluid that nourishes sperm and makes up most of the semen (2 to 5 mL per ejaculate)Infection or blockage can affect fertility
Urethra and penisCarry urine and semen. The penis delivers sperm into the vaginaCondoms act as a barrier here

The sperm pathway is seminiferous tubules, epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct and urethra. FSH and LH from the pituitary control sperm production and testosterone, in the same way they control the female cycle.

Notes on the sources. This topic is standard anatomy and physiology teaching, and I did not look up a separate source for it. Measurements and cycle days are typical values, so check them against your course textbook and lecturer’s notes.

Foetal development.

NSG 403: Maternal and Child Health Nursing I · Topic 6 of 13

Download practice pack:
On this pageStages of prenatal developmentPlacenta, cord, membranes and liquorFetal circulation and the change at birthThe fetal skull and presentationFactors affecting fetal developmentAssessing fetal wellbeing

LO n tags show which course learning outcome each point supports (see the Overview tab). No course outcome covers fetal development directly, so LO 1 is used for the baseline and LO 6 where the content is used in assessment.

Stages of prenatal developmentLO 1

Gestational age is counted from the first day of the last menstrual period, so it is about two weeks more than the time since conception. Development has three periods: the pre-embryonic period (fertilisation to 2 weeks), the embryonic period (weeks 3 to 8 after conception, when organs form) and the fetal period (week 9 to birth, when the fetus grows and matures).

Gestational ageKey developmentMidwifery relevance
By 6 weeksThe neural tube closes and the heart begins to beatFolic acid before conception protects neural tube closure
By 10 weeksAll main organs have formedThe organ-forming period is the time of greatest risk from drugs and infections
12 weeksExternal genitalia differentiate and the kidneys make urineThe fetal heart can be heard with a Doppler device
16 to 20 weeksMovements are first felt (quickening) and fine hair (lanugo) appearsAsk about movements; the fetal heart can be heard with a Pinard stethoscope from about 20 weeks
24 weeksSurfactant production begins and survival with intensive care becomes possibleAntenatal corticosteroids are considered if preterm birth is expected, as in Topic 3
28 weeksEyes open and the lungs can work with supportA preterm baby needs warmth and breathing support
32 to 36 weeksFat is laid down, the lungs mature and lanugo is shedIn a first pregnancy the head often engages around 36 weeks
37 to 42 weeksTerm. The baby is ready for life outside the wombBirth before 37 weeks is preterm

Placenta, cord, membranes and liquorLO 1LO 3

  • The placenta forms from the trophoblast and the maternal decidua. At term it is disc-shaped, about 15 to 20 cm across and about 500 g.
  • Its functions are gas exchange, nutrition, excretion, hormone production (hCG, oestrogen, progesterone), protection and storage. It is not a complete barrier, so many drugs, alcohol, and organisms such as HIV, syphilis and malaria parasites can cross it.
  • The umbilical cord is about 50 cm long and has two arteries, which carry deoxygenated blood to the placenta, and one vein, which carries oxygenated blood to the fetus. Wharton’s jelly protects the vessels.
  • The membranes are the amnion and chorion. Liquor amnii reaches about 800 to 1000 mL at 36 to 37 weeks. It cushions the baby, keeps a steady temperature, allows movement and helps the lungs develop. Too much (polyhydramnios) or too little (oligohydramnios) liquor needs investigation.
  • LO 6After the third stage, check that the placenta and membranes are complete and that the cord has three vessels.

Fetal circulation and the change at birthLO 1LO 8

  • Before birth the lungs are not used, so three shunts divert blood: the ductus venosus (past the liver), the foramen ovale (between the atria) and the ductus arteriosus (from the pulmonary artery to the aorta).
  • Fetal haemoglobin carries oxygen more readily than adult haemoglobin, which helps the fetus take oxygen from the mother’s blood.
  • LO 8At birth the first breath expands the lungs and lowers the resistance to blood flow. The foramen ovale closes, and the ductus arteriosus constricts within hours to days. The ductus venosus closes in the first days. The baby must keep warm and breathing during this change.
  • A normal baseline fetal heart rate is 110 to 160 beats per minute.

The fetal skull and presentationLO 3LO 6

  • The vault bones are two frontal, two parietal and one occipital. They are joined by sutures (sagittal, coronal, lambdoidal and frontal) and are not fused, so they can mould in labour.
  • The anterior fontanelle is diamond-shaped and closes at about 18 months. The posterior fontanelle is triangular and closes at about 6 to 8 weeks.
  • Lie is the relation of the baby’s long axis to the mother’s (usually longitudinal). Presentation is the part at the pelvic brim (usually the head or vertex). Attitude is the posture (flexed is best). Position is where the denominator lies in the pelvis, with left occipito-anterior the commonest.
  • LO 6A well-flexed vertex presents the smallest diameter, so assess lie, presentation and engagement in late pregnancy.

Factors affecting fetal developmentLO 2LO 4LO 10

  • Weeks 3 to 8 after conception are the most sensitive period for birth defects.
  • Alcohol can cause fetal alcohol spectrum disorder, tobacco is linked to low birth weight, and some drugs (for example valproate, warfarin, ACE inhibitors and isotretinoin) can harm the fetus.
  • Infections that cross the placenta include toxoplasmosis, syphilis, rubella, cytomegalovirus, herpes, HIV and malaria (the TORCH group and others).
  • Poor nutrition, folate deficiency and poorly controlled diabetes also affect the baby.
  • LO 2Preconception care and vaccination before pregnancy reduce these risks, as in Topic 1.
  • LO 10Advise women to avoid unprescribed medicines, alcohol and tobacco, and to attend antenatal care early.

Assessing fetal wellbeingLO 6LO 10

  • Ask about fetal movements at every visit and teach the woman to notice her baby’s usual pattern. Reduced or absent movements should be reported the same day, using your facility’s counting method.
  • Measure fundal height (in centimetres it roughly matches the weeks from about 24 to 36 weeks), and listen to the fetal heart rate with a Pinard stethoscope or Doppler.
  • Record findings on the antenatal card and refer if growth, movements or the heart rate are abnormal.
Notes on the sources. This topic is standard embryology and midwifery teaching, and I did not look up separate sources. Gestational ages, sizes and closing times are typical values, so check them against your course textbook and lecturer’s notes.

History of midwifery in Nigeria and globally.

NSG 403: Maternal and Child Health Nursing I · Topic 7 of 13

Download practice pack:
On this pageEarly history of midwiferyMiddle Ages to the nineteenth centuryRegulation and global milestonesHistory in NigeriaThe role of the NMCNWhy history matters today

LO n tags show which course learning outcome each point supports (see the Overview tab). LO 7 (roles of the nurse and midwife) is the closest course outcome, so most points use it.

Early history of midwiferyLO 7

  • Women have helped other women in childbirth since ancient times. The word midwife comes from old English words meaning “with woman”.
  • Early records include the Ebers papyrus of Egypt (about 1550 BC) and the Greek physician Hippocrates. Soranus of Ephesus (around the 2nd century AD) wrote about midwives’ training and qualities.
  • In most societies traditional birth attendants were the main carers, and many learned by apprenticeship.

Middle Ages to the nineteenth centuryLO 7

  • Eucharius Rösslin’s book The Rose Garden (1513) was an early printed guide for midwives.
  • From the 17th and 18th centuries men called man-midwives became involved in childbirth, and instruments such as forceps were developed. William Smellie and William Hunter were leading teachers.
  • In 1847 Ignaz Semmelweis showed that hand washing reduced puerperal fever. Chloroform was first used in labour that year by James Simpson.
  • Midwives had few rules in many places, and deaths from infection and obstructed labour were high.

Regulation and global milestonesLO 7

  • The Midwives Act of 1902 in England set up training and registration for midwives and a Central Midwives Board.
  • The International Confederation of Midwives (ICM) represents midwives worldwide and sets global standards and competencies. It was founded in the early 20th century as the International Midwives Union.
  • The Alma-Ata Declaration (1978) promoted primary health care. The Safe Motherhood Initiative began in Nairobi in 1987 and called for family planning, antenatal care, clean and safe delivery and emergency obstetric care.
  • Millennium Development Goal 5 (2000 to 2015) aimed to cut maternal deaths. Sustainable Development Goal 3 aims for a maternal mortality ratio below 70 per 100,000 live births by 2030.

History in NigeriaLO 7

  • Traditional birth attendants provided most care in communities before and after the colonial period.
  • The colonial government began formal nursing and midwifery training to serve civil servants and their families.
  • The Midwives Ordinance of 1930 set up the Midwives Board to regulate midwifery education and practice. The Nursing Council of Nigeria was set up by the Registration of Nurses Ordinance of 1947.
  • Decree No. 89 of 1979 merged the two bodies into the Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria (NMCN), now governed by the Nursing and Midwifery (Registration, etc.) Act, Cap N143, Laws of the Federation of Nigeria 2004.
  • Nurse and midwife associations that began in the 1930s and 1940s later joined to form the National Association of Nigeria Nurses and Midwives (NANNM).
  • University nursing degrees began in the mid-1960s, and the Midwives Service Scheme of 2009 deployed midwives to primary health care centres.

The role of the NMCNLO 7LO 9

  • Its functions include indexing students, accrediting schools and clinical areas, keeping the register, issuing certificates, setting standards of knowledge and competence, and promoting research.
  • It disciplines members through the Nurses and Midwives Tribunal and prosecutes illegal training institutions.
  • Practitioners must be registered and keep their licence up to date to practise.

Why history matters todayLO 7

  • History shows how regulation, education and evidence improved safety, and why midwives are accountable to the public and the council.
  • Many women still use traditional birth attendants, so respectful partnership with them can support referral and safe care.
Notes on the sources. Nigerian history follows the Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria’s own account (Midwives Ordinance 1930, Registration of Nurses Ordinance 1947, Decree No. 89 of 1979). Some sources give 1949 for the Nursing Council, so check the date in your course text. Global dates, the ICM founding, the first university nursing degree and the Midwives Service Scheme come from standard teaching and should be checked against your notes.
