Ethics and legal issues in midwifery practice.

NSG 403: Maternal and Child Health Nursing I · Topic 8 of 13

Download practice pack:
On this pageEthical principles in midwiferyThe NMCN Code of Professional ConductInformed consentConfidentiality and recordsLegal accountability and relevant lawsEthical dilemmas in midwiferyWomen’s rights in maternity care

LO n tags show which course learning outcome each point supports (see the Overview tab). LO 7 and LO 9 are the closest course outcomes for roles, accountability and documentation.

Ethical principles in midwiferyLO 7LO 10

PrincipleMeaningMidwifery example
AutonomyThe woman’s right to decide about her body and careShe decides on a birth position, pain relief or family planning after being informed
BeneficenceDoing goodGiving timely care and referral
Non-maleficenceDoing no harmAvoiding unnecessary procedures such as routine episiotomy
JusticeFair and equal careTreating every woman respectfully regardless of status, religion or HIV status
VeracityTelling the truthExplaining findings and risks honestly
FidelityKeeping promises and loyaltyStaying with the woman in labour
ConfidentialityProtecting private informationNot discussing her records with others without consent

The NMCN Code of Professional ConductLO 7LO 9

  • The Code places the client at the centre of care and sets out the nurse’s duties to clients, the profession, practice, colleagues, the public and global health bodies.
  • Clients aged 18 and above give informed consent for nursing interventions. For a minor, the next of kin or parents consent.
  • In an emergency, if the client cannot consent, you may give the care needed to preserve life if you can show you acted in the client’s best interest.
  • A professional relationship must be kept. Practitioners are accountable for their actions and for practising within their competence.

Informed consentLO 6LO 10

  • Valid consent needs capacity, enough information (benefits, risks and alternatives) and freedom from pressure.
  • Seek consent for vaginal examinations, episiotomy, caesarean section, family planning, HIV testing and any drug or procedure, and record it.
  • A competent woman may refuse treatment, and the refusal must be respected and recorded after she is told the risks.
  • A woman’s own consent is the ethical basis for her care. Do not make care depend on permission from others.

Confidentiality and recordsLO 9

  • The National Health Act 2014 requires providers to protect the confidentiality of patient information.
  • Share information only with consent, where the law requires it, or where it is necessary to protect others, and only as much as is needed.
  • Keep records accurate, timely, legible and signed. They are legal documents and may be used as evidence.

Legal accountability and relevant lawsLO 7LO 9

  • Negligence needs four things: a duty of care, a breach of that duty, harm caused by the breach, and damage. Employers may share liability for staff actions.
  • The National Health Act 2014 says emergency treatment must not be refused, and refusal can be an offence.
  • The Violence Against Persons (Prohibition) Act 2015 prohibits female genital mutilation and other forms of violence, and the Child Rights Act 2003 protects children’s rights and health.
  • Abortion law in Nigeria is restrictive. The Criminal Code (southern states) and Penal Code (northern states) allow it only to save the woman’s life. Check current law and your state’s rules.
  • Births, stillbirths and deaths must be notified and registered as the law requires.
  • Practise only within your scope of practice, competence and the council’s rules.

Ethical dilemmas in midwiferyLO 4LO 10

  • Examples: a woman who refuses a caesarean section or blood transfusion, conflict between the mother’s wishes and the baby’s wellbeing, an adolescent who wants privacy, and not enough staff or supplies.
  • A simple approach: identify the problem, gather facts, name the principles in conflict, list options, consult the team or senior, decide, act, document and review.
  • Always keep the woman informed, protect her dignity and act in her best interests.

Women’s rights in maternity careLO 10

  • The respectful maternity care charter lists seven rights: freedom from harm and ill-treatment; information, informed consent and respect for choices; privacy and confidentiality; dignity and respect; equality and freedom from discrimination; the highest attainable standard of health care; and liberty and freedom from coercion.
  • Disrespect and abuse includes physical abuse, non-consented care, non-confidential care, discrimination and abandonment. Report and prevent it.
Notes on the sources. The NMCN Code of Professional Conduct (consent, emergency care) and the National Health Act 2014 (emergency care and confidentiality) were checked against NMCN and published summaries. The other laws, the respectful maternity care rights, the elements of negligence and the abortion provisions come from standard teaching and may have changed. Check the current Acts, your state’s rules and your lecturer’s notes before using them in exams or practice.

Theories applicable to midwifery practice.

NSG 403: Maternal and Child Health Nursing I · Topic 9 of 13

Download practice pack:
On this pageWhy use theory in midwiferyNursing theories and their useTheories of maternal role and attachmentApplying theory to careMedical and midwifery models of care

LO n tags show which course learning outcome each point supports (see the Overview tab). No course outcome names theory directly, so tags show where each theory supports assessment (LO 6), documentation and planning (LO 9), and the roles of the midwife (LO 7).

Why use theory in midwiferyLO 7

  • A theory is a set of related ideas that explains or predicts events. A concept is one idea (for example, adaptation) and a model or framework organises concepts.
  • Theory guides assessment, care planning, communication and evaluation, and builds the profession’s knowledge.

Nursing theories and their useLO 6LO 9

TheoristMain ideaMidwifery use
Florence NightingaleA clean, quiet, well-ventilated environment helps healingHygiene, ventilation and a calm labour room
Hildegard PeplauInterpersonal relations. Phases: orientation, identification, exploitation, resolutionBuilding trust with a woman across ANC, labour and postnatal care
Dorothea OremSelf-care deficit. Nursing helps when self-care needs exceed ability (wholly compensatory, partly compensatory, supportive-educative)Teaching a new mother to care for herself and her baby
Callista RoyAdaptation across physiological, self-concept, role function and interdependence modesHelping a woman adapt to pregnancy, birth and motherhood
Betty NeumanSystems model with lines of defence and three levels of preventionAntenatal screening (secondary) and rehabilitation after complications (tertiary)
Imogene KingGoal attainment through interaction and transactionAgreeing goals with the woman in a care plan
Jean WatsonCaring science: caring is the core of nursingRespectful, compassionate care
Madeleine LeiningerTranscultural care that respects cultureCare that fits local beliefs and practices
Nola PenderHealth promotion model: people act to promote their healthAntenatal health education

Theories of maternal role and attachmentLO 3LO 10

  • Reva Rubin’s phases of maternal role: taking-in (first 1 to 2 days, she is passive and needs rest), taking-hold (she begins to care for the baby and needs teaching) and letting-go (she accepts the new role).
  • Ramona Mercer’s maternal role attainment: a woman moves through anticipatory, formal, informal and personal stages.
  • Bowlby and Ainsworth describe attachment, and Klaus and Kennell describe bonding in the first hours after birth. Skin-to-skin contact supports both.
  • Kübler-Ross’s stages of grief (denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance) help in caring for a woman after a perinatal loss. People do not always pass through the stages in order.
  • Maslow’s hierarchy of needs guides priorities: physiological and safety needs come first.

Applying theory to careLO 6LO 9

  • Choose a theory that fits the woman’s problem and setting, assess using its ideas, plan, give care and evaluate.
  • Example: a postnatal mother who is unsure about breastfeeding. Using Orem’s supportive-educative system, assess her knowledge, teach positioning and latch, support her, and evaluate whether she can feed independently.
  • Example: antenatal care with Neuman’s model. Primary prevention is nutrition and tetanus vaccination, secondary prevention is screening for anaemia and pre-eclampsia, and tertiary prevention is rehabilitation after a complication.

Medical and midwifery models of careLO 7LO 10

FeatureMedical modelMidwifery model
View of birthA process with possible pathologyA normal life event
FocusIllness and riskHealth, normality and the whole woman
RelationshipThe professional directs careA partnership with the woman
ContinuityOften different carersContinuity of carer is valued
InterventionUsed readilyUsed only when needed

Good practice uses both. Midwives support normal birth and recognise complications early, then refer.

Notes on the sources. This topic is standard nursing theory teaching, and I did not look up separate sources. Check the names, phases and models against your course textbook and lecturer’s notes, because some courses use different theorists.

Basic concepts of midwifery.

NSG 403: Maternal and Child Health Nursing I · Topic 10 of 13

Download practice pack:
On this pageDefinitionsScope of midwifery practiceRoles and functions of the midwifePhilosophy and principles of careLevels of care and referralMaternal and child health indicators

LO n tags show which course learning outcome each point supports (see the Overview tab). LO 7 (roles of the nurse and midwife) is the closest course outcome.

DefinitionsLO 7

  • Midwifery means being “with woman”. A midwife works in partnership with women to give support, care and advice in pregnancy, labour and the postnatal period, conducts births on her own responsibility, and cares for the newborn and infant.
  • The International Confederation of Midwives (ICM) says this care includes prevention, promoting normal birth, detecting complications in mother and baby, getting medical help, and carrying out emergency measures. It also includes health counselling and education for the woman, her family and the community.
  • A midwife must have completed an accredited midwifery programme and be registered or licensed to practise.

Scope of midwifery practiceLO 7LO 3LO 5LO 8

  • Preconception care, antenatal care, care in labour and birth, postnatal care, newborn care, family planning and adolescent sexual and reproductive health.
  • Community and primary health care work, health education, referral, and working with traditional birth attendants.
  • Scope is limited by training, the law, council rules and what the facility provides. Never practise beyond your competence, and call for help early.

Roles and functions of the midwifeLO 7

  • Clinician: assesses, gives care and detects problems.
  • Educator and counsellor: teaches women and families, and supports informed choices.
  • Advocate: speaks up for the woman’s rights and needs.
  • Manager and coordinator: organises care, supplies and referral, and supervises junior staff.
  • Researcher and leader: uses evidence, takes part in audit and helps improve services.

Philosophy and principles of careLO 7LO 10

  • Woman-centred care with respect for her choices, culture and dignity.
  • Continuity of carer and care across the continuum.
  • Promoting normal birth while recognising complications early.
  • Evidence-based practice and safe, clean care.
  • Partnership with the woman, her family and the health team.

Levels of care and referralLO 7LO 4

  • Basic emergency obstetric and newborn care (BEmONC) has seven signal functions: parenteral antibiotics, uterotonic drugs, parenteral anticonvulsants, manual removal of the placenta, removal of retained products, assisted vaginal birth and basic newborn resuscitation.
  • Comprehensive emergency care (CEmONC) adds caesarean section and blood transfusion.
  • Delays in care are the delay in deciding to seek care, the delay in reaching a facility and the delay in receiving care once there. Good referral reduces all three.
  • LO 4Stabilise the woman, send a written note with her, call ahead and arrange safe transport.

Maternal and child health indicatorsLO 7LO 4

  • A maternal death is the death of a woman while pregnant or within 42 days of the end of pregnancy, from any cause related to or made worse by the pregnancy or its management, but not from accidental causes.
  • The maternal mortality ratio is maternal deaths per 100,000 live births.
  • Neonatal mortality is deaths in the first 28 days per 1000 live births. Perinatal mortality counts stillbirths and early neonatal deaths (the first 7 days).
  • Four pillars of Safe Motherhood: family planning, antenatal care, clean and safe delivery, and essential obstetric care.
Notes on the sources. The midwife definition follows the ICM’s wording in summary, and the BEmONC, maternal death and three delays definitions are from standard WHO-based teaching. I did not look up separate sources, so check them against your textbook and lecturer’s notes.

Standard nursing language and the nursing process.

NSG 403: Maternal and Child Health Nursing I · Topic 11 of 13

Download practice pack:
On this pageThe nursing process in midwiferyAssessmentNursing diagnosisPlanning and implementationEvaluationStandardised nursing languagesDocumentation

LO n tags show which course learning outcome each point supports (see the Overview tab). LO 9 (applying the nursing process and documentation) is the closest course outcome, with LO 6 for assessment.

The nursing process in midwiferyLO 9LO 6

The nursing process is a cycle of assessment, nursing diagnosis, planning, implementation and evaluation. It is client-centred, goal-directed and used to solve problems systematically. Topic 2 showed a worked care plan for a postnatal mother and a newborn.

AssessmentLO 6

  • Subjective data is what the woman tells you (for example “I feel dizzy”). Objective data is what you observe or measure (for example blood pressure 150/100).
  • Collect data by interview (booking history: personal, obstetric, medical, family and social), observation and examination, and by reading records.
  • Check that data is complete and correct, group it and record it. Missing or wrong data leads to wrong diagnoses.

Nursing diagnosisLO 9LO 6

  • A nursing diagnosis describes the woman’s response to a health problem that nurses can treat, unlike a medical diagnosis, which names the disease. Example: the medical diagnosis is pre-eclampsia, and a nursing diagnosis is risk for injury related to seizures.
  • Actual diagnoses use the PES format: problem, related to (etiology), as evidenced by (signs and symptoms). Example: ineffective breastfeeding related to poor latch as evidenced by sore nipples and a crying baby.
  • Risk diagnoses have no signs and symptoms yet. Example: risk for infection related to an episiotomy wound.
  • Health promotion diagnoses show readiness for improvement, such as readiness for enhanced knowledge of newborn care.

Planning and implementationLO 9

  • Set priorities, using life-threatening problems first (airway, breathing, circulation), then urgent and other problems.
  • Write goals that are client-centred, specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound (SMART), with short-term and long-term goals.
  • Interventions can be independent (the nurse decides, such as teaching), dependent (on a prescriber’s order, such as giving a drug) or collaborative (with the team). Give a rationale for each.
  • Carry out the plan, delegate safely, keep the woman informed, and record what you do.

EvaluationLO 9LO 6

  • Compare the woman’s response with the goal and decide whether it was met, partly met or not met.
  • If it was not met, check the assessment, diagnosis, goal and interventions, then revise the plan.
  • Evaluation also covers the quality of care and how the woman feels about it.

Standardised nursing languagesLO 9

  • NANDA-I is a list of nursing diagnoses. The Nursing Interventions Classification (NIC) lists interventions. The Nursing Outcomes Classification (NOC) lists outcomes. Together they link diagnoses, interventions and outcomes.
  • The International Classification for Nursing Practice (ICNP), from the International Council of Nurses, is a global terminology for diagnoses, interventions and outcomes.
  • The Omaha System is another classification used in community nursing.
  • Benefits: nurses communicate clearly, records can be compared, data supports research and quality improvement, and electronic records work better.

DocumentationLO 9

  • Common formats include narrative notes, SOAP (subjective, objective, assessment, plan), SOAPIE (adds intervention and evaluation), PIE (problem, intervention, evaluation) and focus charting (data, action, response).
  • The partograph and the labour care record are standard tools in labour.
  • Records must be accurate, timely, legible and signed with date and time. Correct an error with a single line through it, never erase or use correction fluid.
Notes on the sources. The nursing process, PES format, SOAP and the classification systems (NANDA-I, NIC, NOC, ICNP, Omaha) are standard nursing teaching, and I did not look up separate sources. Check the formats your school uses.

Ethical and legal aspects of HIV/AIDS.

NSG 403: Maternal and Child Health Nursing I · Topic 12 of 13

Download practice pack:
On this pageHIV in pregnancy: key factsEthical principlesLegal framework in NigeriaTesting and counselling in pregnancyPreventing mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT)Family planning and care for women with HIVProtecting health workers and reducing stigma

LO n tags show which course learning outcome each point supports (see the Overview tab). No course outcome covers HIV directly, so tags show where it supports LO 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 10.

HIV in pregnancy: key factsLO 4LO 8

  • HIV is passed by sex, blood, and from mother to child during pregnancy, labour and breastfeeding.
  • Without any prevention, about 15 to 45 percent of babies born to women with HIV become infected. With the interventions below the risk falls below 5 percent.

Ethical principlesLO 7LO 10

  • Autonomy: the woman decides about testing and treatment after being informed.
  • Confidentiality: protect her status. Share it only with her consent or where the law requires.
  • Non-maleficence and beneficence: protect the woman and baby from harm and give the best care.
  • Justice: treat every woman equally and without stigma.
  • WHO’s five Cs for HIV testing: consent, confidentiality, counselling, correct results and connection to care.

Legal framework in NigeriaLO 7

  • The HIV and AIDS (Anti-Discrimination) Act 2014 prohibits discrimination against people living with HIV and protects their access to health care, rights and dignity. It also protects the confidentiality of their status.
  • The National Health Act 2014 protects confidentiality and requires that emergency treatment is not refused.
  • National guidelines say antiretroviral therapy (ART) should be started for all people with HIV, including pregnant and breastfeeding women, whatever the stage of disease.
  • The 2011 national testing guidelines allow some minors (married, pregnant, parents or sexually active) to consent to testing. The law and guidelines change, so check the current version.
  • The NMCN Code of Professional Conduct requires confidentiality and respect for every client.

Testing and counselling in pregnancyLO 6LO 10

  • Offer testing to every pregnant woman at the first antenatal visit with brief pre-test information. She may decline, and care must continue.
  • Give results privately, with post-test counselling and a link to care. Follow the national guideline for repeat testing later in pregnancy, in labour or after birth.
  • Encourage partner testing and support the woman in deciding whether and how to disclose. Never disclose on her behalf without consent.

Preventing mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT)LO 4LO 8

  • The four prongs: prevent HIV in women, prevent unintended pregnancy in women living with HIV, prevent transmission from mother to baby, and give care and support.
  • The woman starts lifelong ART as early as possible and takes it every day. Viral load is checked as the guideline directs.
  • In labour, follow standard precautions and avoid unnecessary invasive procedures. HIV alone is not a reason for caesarean section.
  • LO 8The baby receives ARV prophylaxis from birth as the national guideline directs (for example nevirapine, for a longer time if the risk is high). Early infant diagnosis is done by DNA PCR from about 6 weeks, and cotrimoxazole prophylaxis is given until HIV is excluded.
  • Exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months while the mother takes ART is recommended in settings like Nigeria, then continue with complementary food. Support and counselling are essential.

Family planning and care for women with HIVLO 5LO 10

  • Most women living with HIV can use most contraceptive methods.
  • Advise condoms for dual protection, with another method for pregnancy prevention.
  • Check for interactions between ART and hormonal methods with the prescriber.

Protecting health workers and reducing stigmaLO 6LO 7

  • Use standard precautions with all clients, handle sharps safely and dispose of them in a box.
  • After an exposure, wash the area, report it and start post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) as soon as possible and within 72 hours.
  • Refusing care to a woman because she has HIV is discrimination. Labelling files, delaying care and breaching confidentiality are examples of stigma to avoid.
Notes on the sources. The Nigerian legal points were checked against published summaries of the HIV and AIDS (Anti-Discrimination) Act 2014, the National Health Act 2014 and the national HIV guidelines. Prophylaxis regimens, the transmission rates, testing age rules and the PEP timing come from WHO-based standard teaching and change over time. Check the current Nigerian national HIV guidelines and your lecturer’s notes before using this in exams or practice.

Quality of care in midwifery practice.

NSG 403: Maternal and Child Health Nursing I · Topic 13 of 13

Download practice pack:
On this pageWhat is quality of care?The WHO framework and standardsExperience of care and respectful maternity careSafety and infection preventionMethods for improving qualityQuality indicatorsThe midwife’s role in quality

LO n tags show which course learning outcome each point supports (see the Overview tab). No course outcome covers quality of care directly, so tags show where it supports LO 6, 7, 9 and 10.

What is quality of care?LO 7

  • Quality of care means care that is safe, effective, woman-centred, timely, efficient and equitable.
  • Donabedian’s model looks at structure (staff, equipment, buildings), process (what is done) and outcome (what results for the woman and baby).

The WHO framework and standardsLO 7LO 9

  • WHO’s 2016 framework has eight domains of quality, covering the provision of care and the experience of care, supported by the health system. It has eight standards.
  • Provision of care: evidence-based routine care and management of complications, actionable information systems and functional referral systems.
  • Experience of care: effective communication, respect, protection and dignity, and emotional support.
  • Cross-cutting: competent, motivated staff, and essential physical resources such as water, sanitation, energy, medicines and equipment.

Experience of care and respectful maternity careLO 10

  • Good communication means explaining what is happening, listening and using the woman’s language.
  • Respect and dignity include privacy, consent, a companion of choice and freedom from abuse.
  • Emotional support reduces fear and helps the woman cope with labour.
  • Women’s experience affects whether they return to the facility for care.

Safety and infection preventionLO 6

  • Hand hygiene at the five moments, clean gloves and a clean delivery surface, safe sharps handling, and proper cleaning and sterilisation of equipment.
  • Safe waste disposal and a clean environment. Sepsis is a major cause of maternal and newborn death, and it is largely preventable.
  • Use checklists, for example the WHO Safe Childbirth Checklist, at admission, before pushing, after birth and before discharge.

Methods for improving qualityLO 9

  • Clinical audit: set a standard, measure practice, compare, change and re-audit.
  • The Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) cycle tests small changes and keeps those that work.
  • Maternal and perinatal death surveillance and response (MPDSR) reviews deaths to find avoidable factors and act on them.
  • Supportive supervision, mentoring, guidelines and regular data review keep standards up.

Quality indicatorsLO 7LO 9

  • Outcome and process measures include the maternal mortality ratio, stillbirth and neonatal mortality, caesarean section rate, use of the partograph or labour care guide, early skin-to-skin contact and breastfeeding, birth-dose vaccines, uterotonic given to every woman, and attendance at antenatal care (WHO now advises 8 contacts).
  • Client satisfaction and reports of disrespect also measure quality.

The midwife’s role in qualityLO 7LO 9LO 10

  • Follow protocols and current evidence, document accurately and escalate problems early.
  • Communicate respectfully, keep the woman informed and protect her rights.
  • Take part in audit, death reviews and team meetings, and keep skills up to date through continuing education.
  • Advocate for supplies, staffing and a safe environment.
Notes on the sources. The WHO framework and standards were checked against WHO’s 2016 publication summaries. Donabedian’s model, the indicators, the Safe Childbirth Checklist, PDSA and MPDSR come from standard teaching, and I did not look up separate sources. Check them against your lecturer’s notes.
